Whole grains and chronic disease risk


risk of incident breast cancer was 20% higher for women with the highest, vs. lowest whole grain intake. However, when the data
were further examined, it appeared that the incidence of breast cancer was not higher among women who had not undergone
screening mammography before follow-up. This suggests that increasing whole grain intake was associated with more health-
conscious behaviors such as attending cancer screening, thus increasing the detection rate in whole grain consumers. In a cohort
of Danish post-menopausal women, no protective association was observed between whole grain intake and breast cancer risk,
including all estrogen and progesterone receptor disease subtypes. It is possible that hormone replacement therapy may interfere
with the mechanisms of lignans/enterolactone with higher whole grain intake.
A 2018 meta-analysis of data from 11 published studies (4 cohort and 7 case-control) suggested that, compared to the lowest
intake, those with the highest whole grain intake had 16% lower risk of breast cancer (pooled RR 0.84, 95% CI: 0.74–0.96,
